parts.text: Find the possible integer values of a.

A1: Obtains the other valid value a=-4.

text: Five named sheep are placed in six pens arranged as a 3 by 2 grid. Amber and Brownie must be separated. (a) Pens may contain multiple sheep; Amber and Brownie cannot share a pen. (b) Each pen may contain one sheep; Amber and Brownie cannot occupy pens sharing a boundary. Count the placements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Count placements when pens may hold multiple sheep and Amber and Brownie are in different pens.
parts.scheme: M1: Accounts for the restriction that the second of Amber and Brownie has one fewer pen choice, or subtracts the together cases. A1: Counts the ordered placements of Amber and Brownie as 6×5, or an equivalent complementary count. A1: Gives each of the other three sheep six independent pen choices. A1: Obtains 5×6⁴=6480 placements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Count one-sheep-per-pen placements when Amber and Brownie do not share a boundary.
parts.scheme: A1: Counts all one-sheep-per-pen placements as 6!=720, or an equivalent complete case total. A1: Counts 336 placements in which Amber and Brownie occupy adjacent pens, or obtains the equivalent permitted-case subtotals. M1: Subtracts prohibited adjacent placements from the total, or adds the complete permitted cases. A1: Obtains 384 placements.

text: Two biased four-sided dice have probability distributions X: p,p,p,p/2 for scores 1,2,3,4 and Y: q,q,q,r for scores 1,2,3,4. Determine p, E(X), the possible ranges of r, q and E(Y), then use P(X<Y)=1/2 to find E(Y).

parts.label: a
parts.scheme: M1: Uses that the probabilities p+p+p+p/2 sum to 1. A1: Obtains p=2/7.

parts.label: b
parts.scheme: M1: Forms the expected-value sum 1p+2p+3p+4(p/2). A1: Obtains E(X)=16/7.

parts.label: c.i
parts.text: State the possible range of r.
parts.scheme: A1: States 0≤r≤1.

parts.label: c.ii
parts.text: Find the possible range of q.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses 3q+r=1 and the probability bounds to derive bounds for q. A1: States 0≤q≤1/3.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the possible range of E(Y).
parts.scheme: A1: Expresses E(Y)=q+2q+3q+4r, equivalently 2+2r or 4-6q. A1: Evaluates a correct boundary value of E(Y). A1: States 2≤E(Y)≤4.

parts.label: e
parts.scheme: M1: Identifies at least four correct ordered outcomes contributing to X<Y. A1: Forms a correct probability expression for P(X<Y), using independence of the two die rolls. M1: Sets the probability expression equal to 1/2 and solves for q, r or directly for E(Y). A2: Obtains q=5/24 and r=3/8, or the equivalent two correct intermediate values required by the selected method. A1: Obtains E(Y)=11/4.

text: For L1 defined by (x+1)/2=y=3-z, verify (-1,0,3), find a vector equation, determine the parameter a when its acute angle with L2:r=(0,1,2)+t(a,1,-1) is 45 degrees, and determine the exceptional value k and the intersection point A in terms of a.

parts.label: a.i
parts.scheme: A1: Substitutes (-1,0,3) into the Cartesian equation and verifies all three expressions are zero.

parts.label: a.ii
parts.text: Find a vector equation of L1.
parts.scheme: M1: Introduces a common parameter for the Cartesian form. A1: Obtains a correct direction vector proportional to (2,1,-1). A1: Gives r=(-1,0,3)+lambda(2,1,-1), or an equivalent vector equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the possible values of a when the acute angle between L1 and L2 is 45 degrees.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the scalar-product formula for the angle between the direction vectors. A1: Forms the correct dot product 2a+2. A1: Forms the correct product of vector magnitudes sqrt(6)sqrt(a^2+2). A1: Includes the acute-angle absolute-value sign or equivalent plus-or-minus relation. A1: Uses cos 45 degrees=sqrt(2)/2 and simplifies the angle equation correctly. A1: Obtains the quadratic a^2+8a-2=0. M1: Solves the resulting quadratic equation. A1: Obtains a=-4 plus or minus 3sqrt(2).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find k and the coordinates of the unique intersection A in terms of a.
parts.scheme: M1: Equates the parametric coordinate equations of L1 and L2. A1: Writes a correct simultaneous system for lambda and t. M1: Eliminates a parameter to obtain an equation containing the factor a-2. A1: Identifies the exceptional value k=2. A1: Obtains t=1/(a-2) or lambda=(a-1)/(a-2). A2: Obtains A=(a/(a-2),(a-1)/(a-2),(2a-5)/(a-2)).

text: For f(x)=sqrt(1+x), prove the stated nth-derivative formula by induction and use the Maclaurin coefficient of x^2 in h(x)=sqrt(1+x)e^(mx) to determine m.

parts.label: a
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the chain rule to differentiate sqrt(1+x). A1: Obtains f'(x)=1/(2sqrt(1+x)). A1: Obtains f''(x)=-1/(4(1+x)^(3/2)).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use mathematical induction to prove the stated formula for f^(n)(x), n at least 2.
parts.scheme: R1: Verifies the base case n=2 using the result from part a. M1: States the induction hypothesis correctly for n=k. M1: Considers n=k+1 by differentiating the kth derivative. A1: Differentiates the power of 1+x correctly. A1: Writes the target factorial expression for the k+1 case. A1: Expands and simplifies the factorial ratio correctly. A1: Extracts the required factor -1/4 correctly. A1: Obtains exactly the stated formula with n replaced by k+1. R1: Completes the induction argument for all integers n at least 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Given the x^2 coefficient of h(x)=f(x)e^(mx) is 7/4, find m.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the product rule to form derivatives of h, or an equivalent Maclaurin-product method. A1: Obtains a correct expression for h'(x) or the linear series terms. A1: Obtains a correct expression for h''(x) or the x^2 coefficient before substitution. M1: Evaluates the second derivative information at x=0. A1: Obtains h''(0)=m^2+m-1/4. M1: Equates h''(0)/2 to 7/4. A1: Obtains 4m^2+4m-15=0. A1: Obtains m=-5/2 or m=3/2.

solution.outline: The derivative formula follows by the n=2 base case and the k to k+1 step; m=-5/2 or 3/2.

text: Given dy/dx=cos(x-pi/4) and y=2 when x=3pi/4, find y in terms of x.

parts.label: main
parts.text: Integrate the derivative and apply the given point.

text: Prove by induction the stated nth derivative of x^2e^x, use it to obtain the Maclaurin series through x^4, and evaluate lim as x approaches 0 of ((x^2e^x-x^2)^3)/x^9.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove the nth-derivative formula by induction.
parts.scheme: A1: Differentiates x^2e^x correctly for the n=1 base case. A1: Shows the right-hand formula agrees when n=1. M1: States the induction hypothesis correctly for n=k. M1: Differentiates the induction-hypothesis expression to form the k+1 case. A1: Applies the product rule correctly in the k+1 differentiation. A1: Simplifies to [x^2+2(k+1)x+k(k+1)]e^x. parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the Maclaurin series of x^2e^x through x^4.

parts.label: c

text: Solve and represent the roots of (z-1)^3=i, plot them on an Argand diagram, find AC, then study (z-1)^3=iz^3 to verify alpha=1/(1-e^(i pi/6)) and determine Re(alpha).

parts.label: a.i
parts.text: Verify omega1=1+e^(i pi/6) is a root.
parts.scheme: A1: Substitutes omega1 and reduces (omega1-1)^3 to (e^(i pi/6))^3. A1: Uses exponential or trigonometric form to obtain i.

parts.label: a.ii
parts.text: Find omega2 and omega3 in translated exponential form.
parts.scheme: M1: Writes i with its full family of arguments before taking cube roots. M1: Divides the arguments by three and applies the translation z=1+(z-1). A1: Obtains omega2=1+e^(i5pi/6). A1: Obtains omega3=1+e^(i9pi/6), equivalently 1-i.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Plot A, B and C on an Argand diagram.
parts.scheme: M1: Converts the three roots to Cartesian coordinates or correctly translates their unit-circle positions. A1: Plots A at (1+sqrt(3)/2,1/2). A1: Plots B at (1-sqrt(3)/2,1/2). A1: Plots C at (1,-1).

parts.label: c
parts.scheme: M1: Forms the complex difference omega1-omega3 or the coordinate displacement AC. M1: Computes the modulus sqrt(3/4+9/4). A1: Obtains AC=sqrt(3).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use de Moivre's theorem to verify the stated alpha root.
parts.scheme: M1: Divides by z^3 to obtain ((z-1)/z)^3=i and applies de Moivre's theorem. A1: Obtains (alpha-1)/alpha=e^(i pi/6), or the equivalent reciprocal form. A1: Rearranges to alpha=1/(1-e^(i pi/6)).

parts.label: e
parts.scheme: M1: Writes e^(i pi/6) in Cartesian form. A1: Obtains a correct Cartesian denominator, such as 2-sqrt(3)-i after scaling. M1: Uses the complex conjugate to rationalize the denominator. A1: Forms the correct conjugate-product numerator. A1: Simplifies the real component of alpha correctly. A1: Obtains Re(alpha)=1/2.

Shows convergence because the common-ratio magnitude is 1/sqrt(3), which is less than 1, considering both signs. Uses the infinite geometric-series sum with first term ln(x) and ratio 1/sqrt(3). Obtains ln(x)=2. Obtains x=e^2. Uses equal consecutive differences or the arithmetic-mean relation. Forms a correct equation relating p ln(x), ln(x), and one-third ln(x). Simplifies to 2p=4/3 and obtains p=2/3. Obtains d=-(1/3)ln(x). Substitutes the first term and common difference into the arithmetic-series sum and equates it to ln(1/x^3). Rewrites ln(1/x^3) as ln(x^-3). Simplifies ln(x^-3) to -3ln(x). Carries out correct algebra with S_n. Cancels ln(x) and obtains a correct equation in n. Forms the quadratic n^2-7n-18=0 or an equivalent equation. Solves the quadratic, for example by factorizing (n-9)(n+2). Selects the valid term count n=9.

text: For three given planes, show that they have no common intersection, find the line of intersection of the first two planes through P(1,-2,0), and find the distance from that line to the third plane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the three planes do not intersect.
parts.scheme: M1: Eliminates a variable from the plane equations or begins an equivalent valid consistency test. A1: Obtains one correct reduced equation in two variables. A1: Obtains an incompatible reduced equation with the same left-hand side and a different constant. R1: Identifies the contradiction and concludes that the three planes have no common intersection.

parts.label: b.i
parts.text: Verify that P(1,-2,0) lies on both Pi1 and Pi2.
parts.scheme: A1: Substitutes P(1,-2,0) and verifies both Pi1 and Pi2 equations.

parts.label: b.ii
parts.text: Find a vector equation of the line of intersection of Pi1 and Pi2.
parts.scheme: M1: Attempts the vector product of the normals to Pi1 and Pi2, or an equivalent parameter-elimination method. A1: Obtains a valid direction vector such as (1,5,3). A1: Uses a valid point on the line, such as P(1,-2,0), as the position vector. A1: States a complete vector equation, for example r=(1,-2,0)+lambda(1,5,3).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the distance between the intersection line and Pi3.
parts.scheme: M1: Constructs a line through P in the normal direction (-9,3,-2) of Pi3, or starts the equivalent parallel-plane method. A1: States the correct perpendicular-line equation through P. M1: Substitutes the perpendicular line into Pi3 or forms the corresponding parallel plane through P. A1: Obtains the intersection parameter t=1/2 or the equivalent plane constant -15. M1: Uses the three-dimensional distance between P and the perpendicular intersection point, or the distance between parallel planes. A1: Obtains the distance sqrt(94)/2.

solution.outline: The plane equations are inconsistent, so there is no common intersection. P lies on Pi1 and Pi2; their line is r=(1,-2,0)+lambda(1,5,3), and its distance from Pi3 is sqrt(94)/2.

text: Find Maclaurin expansions for e^x sin(x) and e^x cos(x), use one expansion for an approximate definite integral, derive recurrence relations for higher derivatives, and evaluate a limit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the Maclaurin series for e^x sin(x) through x^3.
parts.scheme: M1: Recognizes the known Maclaurin series for e^x and sin(x), or begins an equivalent derivative method. M1: Multiplies the series consistently through the x^3 term. A1: Obtains the unsimplified coefficients x+x^2+(-1/6+1/2)x^3. A1: Obtains e^x sin(x)=x+x^2+(1/3)x^3+....

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the series to approximate the integral from 0 to 1 of e^(x^2)sin(x^2) dx.
parts.scheme: A1: Substitutes x^2 into the series to obtain x^2+x^4+(1/3)x^6+.... M1: Sets up and integrates the truncated series from 0 to 1. A1: Obtains the antiderivative x^3/3+x^5/5+x^7/21. A1: Obtains the approximation 61/105.

parts.label: c.i
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the product rule at least once for g=e^x cos(x). A1: Obtains g'=e^x cos(x)-e^x sin(x). A1: Obtains g''=-2e^x sin(x). A1: Shows that 2(g'-g) equals g''.

parts.label: c.ii
parts.scheme: A1: Differentiates the relation twice in total to obtain g^(4)=2(g'''-g'').

parts.label: d
parts.text: Using part (c), find the Maclaurin series for g through x^4.
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes x=0 into a derivative relation from part (c). A1: Obtains g(0)=1, g'(0)=1, and g''(0)=0. A1: Uses part (c) to obtain g'''(0)=-2 and g^(4)(0)=-4. M1: Substitutes the derivative values into the Maclaurin formula. A1: Obtains g(x)=1+x-(1/3)x^3-(1/6)x^4+....

parts.label: e
parts.text: Evaluate the stated limit as x tends to 0.
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes the series into the limit or correctly begins repeated l'Hopital evaluation. A1: Cancels 1+x and divides by x^3 to obtain -1/3-(1/6)x+.... A1: Obtains the limit -1/3.

solution.outline: e^x sin(x)=x+x^2+x^3/3+...; the integral is approximately 61/105; g''=2(g'-g) and g^(4)=2(g'''-g''); e^x cos(x)=1+x-x^3/3-x^4/6+...; the limit is -1/3.

text: For the consecutive integers n-1, n, n+1, prove that their sum is divisible by 3 and that the sum of their squares is never divisible by 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prove that the sum of the three integers is divisible by 3.
parts.scheme: A1: Forms (n-1)+n+(n+1). A1: Simplifies to 3n and concludes divisibility by 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Prove that the sum of their squares is never divisible by 3.
parts.scheme: A1: Forms (n-1)^2+n^2+(n+1)^2. M1: Correctly expands the squared consecutive-integer terms. A1: Simplifies the sum to 3n^2+2. R1: Explains that 3n^2 is divisible by 3 but the remainder 2 is not, so the sum is never divisible by 3.

solution.outline: The integer sum is 3n. The square sum is 3n^2+2, which has remainder 2 modulo 3.

text: Use polar complex numbers and an Argand triangle to establish right-angle and equilateral-triangle results, connect the equilateral condition to the coefficients of a quadratic with complex roots, and prove uniqueness for a specified quadratic.

parts.label: a
parts.scheme: A1: Writes conjugate(z2)=r2e^(-i theta). A1: Multiplies to obtain r1r2e^(i(alpha-theta)).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use a zero real part to show the triangle is right-angled.
parts.scheme: A1: Uses Re(z1 conjugate(z2))=r1r2 cos(alpha-theta)=0. A1: Uses 0<alpha-theta<pi to obtain alpha-theta=pi/2 and hence a right angle.

parts.label: c.i
parts.text: For the equilateral case, express z1 in terms of z2.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses equal moduli and the pi/3 angular separation of an equilateral triangle. A1: Obtains z1=z2e^(i pi/3).

parts.label: c.ii
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes z1=z2e^(i pi/3) into z1^2+z2^2. A1: Factors the expression as z2^2(e^(i2pi/3)+1). A1: Uses e^(i2pi/3)+1=e^(i pi/3). A1: Concludes z1^2+z2^2=z1z2.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use the result to show a^2-3b=0.
parts.scheme: A1: Uses z1+z2=-a and z1z2=b. A1: Expands a^2=(z1+z2)^2=z1^2+z2^2+2z1z2. A1: Uses the equilateral identity to obtain a^2=3z1z2. M1: Substitutes b=z1z2. A1: Obtains a^2-3b=0.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Deduce that only one permitted equilateral triangle can be formed for z^2+az+12=0.
parts.scheme: A1: Uses b=12 to obtain a=plus or minus 6 and the two candidate quadratics. R1: Rejects a=-6 because its ordered root-angle difference does not satisfy 0<alpha-theta<pi. A1: Shows a=6 gives the permitted pi/3 separation, so exactly one triangle is possible.

solution.outline: The polar product gives the angular separation; a zero real part gives a right angle. In the equilateral case z1=z2e^(i pi/3) and z1^2+z2^2=z1z2, implying a^2=3b. For b=12 only a=6 satisfies the required ordered angle, so one triangle is possible.

text: A circle has diameter endpoints A(1,4,0) and B(-3,2,-4). Find its centre and radius, then find the exact volume of the right circular cone with this circle as base and vertex V(-1,-1,0).

parts.label: a.i
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the centre of the circle.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the midpoint of A and B for the circle centre. A1: Obtains the centre (-1,3,-2).

parts.label: a.ii
parts.text: Find the radius of the circle.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the three-dimensional distance from the centre to A or half the distance AB. A1: Obtains the radius 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact volume of the right circular cone.
parts.scheme: M1: Calculates the perpendicular cone height as the distance from V to the circle centre. A1: Obtains the height sqrt(20)=2sqrt(5). A1: Uses V=(1/3)pi r^2h to obtain 6pi sqrt(5).

solution.outline: The centre is (-1,3,-2), the radius is 3, the height is 2sqrt(5), and the cone volume is 6pi sqrt(5).

text: Count three-digit codes formed from 1 to 5 with and without repetition. Then, for P(x)=x^3+ax^2+bx+c with distinct a,b,c in that set and factor x^2+3x+2, determine the coefficients, factor P fully and sketch its graph.

parts.text: Count codes when repetition is allowed.
parts.scheme: A1: Forms 5^3 for the repeated-value count. A1: Obtains 125 codes.

parts.label: a.ii
parts.text: Count codes when repetition is not allowed.
parts.scheme: A1: Forms 5P3=5 times 4 times 3. A1: Obtains 60 codes.

parts.label: b.i
parts.text: Find b in terms of a.
parts.scheme: A1: Factors x^2+3x+2 as (x+1)(x+2), or uses an equivalent coefficient setup. M1: Uses the factor theorem or an equivalent polynomial-factor method. parts.text: Show that a=4, b=5 and c=2 is the only assignment.
parts.scheme: R1: Rules out a=1,2,5 because they give invalid b values, or uses the equivalent c relation. R1: Rules out a=3 and concludes uniquely a=4, b=5, c=2.

parts.label: b.iii
parts.text: Express P(x) as a product of linear factors.

parts.label: b.i

parts.label: c

text: A pole of variable angle alpha spans a perpendicular passageway of width 3/4 m and room of width 6 m. Derive its length, use first and second derivatives to find the minimum possible length, and decide whether an 11.25 m pole can pass horizontally.

parts.label: a
parts.scheme: A1: Uses the 3/4 m width to obtain AC=(3/4)sec(alpha). A1: Uses the 6 m width to obtain CB=6cosec(alpha) and hence the stated L.

parts.label: b.i
parts.scheme: A1: Obtains dL/dalpha=(3/4)sec(alpha)tan(alpha)-6cosec(alpha)cot(alpha).

parts.label: b.ii
parts.text: Show the stationary angle is alpha=arctan(2).
parts.scheme: M1: Rewrites the derivative in sine, cosine or tangent form. A1: Sets the derivative to zero and obtains an equation equivalent to (3/4)tan^3(alpha)-6=0. A1: Obtains tan^3(alpha)=8. A1: Obtains tan(alpha)=2 and hence alpha=arctan(2) in the stated interval.

parts.label: c.i
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the product rule in differentiating the first derivative. A1: Correctly differentiates the secant-tangent contribution. A1: Correctly differentiates the cosecant-cotangent contribution.

parts.label: c.ii
parts.text: Evaluate the second derivative at alpha=arctan(2).
parts.scheme: M1: Uses alpha=arctan(2) to obtain an additional exact trigonometric ratio. A1: Obtains correct ratios such as sec(alpha)=sqrt(5), cosec(alpha)=sqrt(5)/2 and cot(alpha)=1/2. A1: Substitutes at least two correct terms into the second derivative. A1: Obtains d^2L/dalpha^2=(45sqrt(5))/4.

parts.label: d.i
parts.text: Justify that L is a minimum at this angle.
parts.scheme: R1: Uses the positive second derivative together with the stationary condition to justify a minimum.

parts.label: d.ii
parts.text: Find the minimum value of L.
parts.scheme: A1: Substitutes the exact trigonometric values into L. A1: Obtains L_min=15sqrt(5)/4 metres.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Determine whether an 11.25 m pole can be carried through horizontally.
parts.scheme: R1: Compares 11.25=15sqrt(9)/4 with 15sqrt(5)/4 and identifies the pole as longer than the limiting length. A1: Concludes that the pole cannot be carried horizontally through the corner.

solution.outline: The stationary angle is alpha=arctan(2), where the second derivative is 45sqrt(5)/4>0 and the minimum clearance length is 15sqrt(5)/4 m. Since 11.25 m is larger, the pole cannot pass horizontally.

text: Two intersecting lines L1 and L2 meet at P. Point A=(2t,8,3), t>0, lies on L2; the acute angle between the lines is pi/3, the direction vector of L1 is (1,1,0), and PA=(2t,0,3+t). Prove the stated equation, find t and the shortest distance from A to L1, find a normal to the plane containing both lines, and find the two possible vertices of a right cone whose base is centred at A and tangent to L1.

parts.label: a
parts.scheme: A1: Calculates the dot product of the direction vectors as 2t. A1: Calculates the required vector magnitudes, including |(1,1,0)|=sqrt(2) and |PA|=sqrt(5t^2+6t+9). M1: Substitutes the vectors and angle pi/3 into the dot-product angle formula. A1: Rearranges the angle equation to 4t=sqrt(10t^2+12t+18).

parts.label: b
parts.scheme: A1: Squares and rearranges to a correct quadratic equation, equivalent to t^2-2t-3=0. M1: Attempts to solve the quadratic equation. A1: Obtains the candidate roots t=3 and t=-1. A1: Uses t>0 to select t=3.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the shortest distance from A to L1.
parts.scheme: M1: Recognizes that the shortest segment from A to L1 is perpendicular to L1, or uses an equivalent vector distance formula. A1: Uses t=3 to obtain PA=(6,0,6) and |PA|=6sqrt(2), or an equivalent correct vector quantity. A1: Uses the angle pi/3, a cross product, a projection, or an equivalent perpendicular-distance calculation correctly. A1: Obtains the shortest distance sqrt(54)=3sqrt(6).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find a normal vector to the plane containing L1 and L2.
parts.scheme: M1: Attempts the vector product of direction vectors (1,1,0) and (6,0,6). A1: Obtains a normal vector proportional to (1,-1,-1), stated in vector form.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the two possible positions of the cone vertex.
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes the base radius 3sqrt(6) into the cone-volume formula and equates it to 90pi sqrt(3). A1: Obtains the cone height h=5sqrt(3). M1: Recognizes that a vertex lies from A in either normal direction to the plane. M1: Relates the scalar multiple of the normal vector to the cone height, or forms the corresponding unit-normal height vector. A1: Obtains scalar displacement mu=plus or minus 5, equivalently height vectors plus or minus (5,-5,-5). A1: Obtains one vertex, (11,3,-2). A1: Obtains the other vertex, (1,13,8).

text: For x at least 0, the region under y=x/(x^2+2) from x=0 to x=c has area ln(3). Find c.

parts.label: main
parts.text: Find c from the stated area condition.
parts.scheme: M1: Attempts the integration by inspection or a substitution such as u=x^2+2. A1: Obtains the correct logarithmic antiderivative and limits, such as [(1/2)ln(x^2+2)] from 0 to c. A1: Obtains an equation equivalent to (c^2+2)/2=9, hence c^2=16. A1: Uses c at least 0 to obtain c=4.

solution.outline: The area integral is (1/2)[ln(c^2+2)-ln(2)]=ln(3), which gives c=4.

text: Use mathematical induction to prove that the sum from r=1 to n of r/(r+1)! equals 1-1/(n+1)! for all integers n at least 1.

text: A triangle with vertices P=(-3,0), Q=(x,y) and R=(x,-y) is inscribed in x^2+y^2=9, with Q and R in the first and fourth quadrants. Express its area in x, derive the stated derivative, and find the y-coordinate of R when the area is maximal.

parts.label: a

text: For u=-1+sqrt(3)i, determine its exponential form and powers; use it to solve related cubic equations and a reciprocal-variable transformation; then solve z^2=2 conjugate(z) in Cartesian form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the modulus and argument of u and show its exponential form.
parts.scheme: A1: Calculates |u|=sqrt((-1)^2+(sqrt(3))^2)=2. M1: Finds the reference angle pi/3 and accounts for the second quadrant. A1: Obtains arg(u)=2pi/3 and hence u=2e^(2pi i/3).

parts.label: b.i
parts.text: Find the least positive n for which u^n is real.
parts.scheme: M1: Requires the imaginary part of u^n to vanish, equivalently 2npi/3=kpi. A1: Recognizes that a multiple of 3 must be considered for n. A1: Obtains the least positive value n=3.

parts.label: b.ii
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes n=3 into the polar or exponential power expression. A1: Obtains u^3=8.

parts.label: c.i
parts.text: Find the other roots of z^3+5z^2+10z+12=0.
parts.scheme: A1: Uses the conjugate-root theorem to identify -1-sqrt(3)i as a root. M1: Uses a valid root-sum, root-product, factorization, or coefficient-comparison method to find the real root. A1: Forms a correct relation using the known conjugate pair, such as (-1+sqrt(3)i)+(-1-sqrt(3)i)+c=-5. A1: Simplifies the selected relation correctly, such as -2+c=-5 or 4c=-12. A1: Obtains the third root z=-3.

parts.label: c.ii
parts.scheme: A1: Recognizes the reciprocal transformation z=1/w, equivalently w=1/z, or earns the paired two-mark transformation credit. A1: Correctly applies the reciprocal transformation to the known roots, or correctly factorizes the polynomial in w. A1: Obtains the real root w=-1/3. A1: Obtains the complex roots w=(-1+sqrt(3)i)/4 and w=(-1-sqrt(3)i)/4.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Solve z^2=2 conjugate(z), z non-zero, using z=a+bi.
parts.scheme: A1: Substitutes z=a+bi and conjugate(z)=a-bi into the equation. M1: Expands and equates real and imaginary parts to obtain a^2-b^2=2a and 2ab=-2b. M1: Uses 2b(a+1)=0 and the real equation to solve the resulting cases. A1: From b=0 and z non-zero, obtains the real root z=2. A1: From a=-1, obtains b=plus or minus sqrt(3) and roots z=-1 plus or minus sqrt(3)i.

solution.outline: u=2e^(2pi i/3), the least n is 3 and u^3=8. The first cubic has roots -3 and -1 plus or minus sqrt(3)i; the reciprocal cubic has roots -1/3 and (-1 plus or minus sqrt(3)i)/4. The final equation has roots 2 and -1 plus or minus sqrt(3)i.

text: Evaluate the integral of cos(sqrt(x)) by substitution and integration by parts. For the curve y=cos(sqrt(x)), use consecutive x-intercepts to find the area of the nth region and prove the region areas form an arithmetic sequence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show the stated antiderivative using an appropriate substitution.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the substitution t=sqrt(x). A1: Obtains x=t^2 and dx=2t dt. A1: Transforms the integral to 2 integral t cos(t) dt. M1: Attempts integration by parts with a valid choice of u and dv. A1: Obtains 2t sin(t)-2 integral sin(t) dt. A1: Integrates and substitutes back to obtain 2sqrt(x)sin(sqrt(x))+2cos(sqrt(x))+C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the area of region R_n.
parts.scheme: M1: Represents the area as the absolute value of the definite integral from x_n to x_(n+1). A1: Uses the antiderivative from part (a) with the correct symbolic limits. M1: Attempts to substitute both intercept limits into the antiderivative. A1: Obtains the correct trigonometric endpoint expression involving (2n+1)pi/2 and (2n-1)pi/2. A1: Correctly evaluates the endpoint sine and cosine values using alternating signs. A1: Combines the endpoint terms correctly inside the absolute value. A1: Applies the absolute value and obtains area(R_n)=4n pi.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Show the region areas form an arithmetic sequence.
parts.scheme: M1: Forms the consecutive-area difference R_(n+1)-R_n or compares R_n with the general arithmetic-sequence form. A1: Obtains the constant difference 4pi. R1: Concludes from the constant difference that the region areas form an arithmetic sequence.

solution.outline: The antiderivative is 2sqrt(x)sin(sqrt(x))+2cos(sqrt(x))+C; x_(n+1)=((2n+1)^2 pi^2)/4; area(R_n)=4n pi; the areas have constant difference 4pi.

text: Prove by mathematical induction that 5^(2n)-2^(3n) is divisible by 17 for every positive integer n.

A1: Rewrites the expression as 25·5^(2k)-8·2^(3k). A1: Adds and subtracts a suitable term so that the induction hypothesis can be used. A1: Expresses the n=k+1 case as a multiple of 17. R1: Concludes that the base case and induction step prove the result for all positive integers n.

parts.text: Find the indefinite integral of x(ln x)^2.

M1: Applies integration by parts a second time to the integral of x ln x. A1: Obtains the integral of x ln x as x^2 ln x/2-x^2/4. A1: Obtains x^2(ln x)^2/2-x^2 ln x/2+x^2/4+C.

text: The functions are f(x)=ln(2x-9), x>9/2, and g(x)=2ln x-ln d, x>0, d>0. State the vertical asymptote of g. Given that the graphs intersect at two distinct points, derive the intersection quadratic, determine the possible values of d, and for d=10 find the distance between the two intersection x-values.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the vertical asymptote of y=g(x).
parts.scheme: A1: States the vertical asymptote x=0.

parts.label: b.i
parts.text: Show that the intersection x-values satisfy x^2-2dx+9d=0.
parts.scheme: M1: Sets ln(2x-9)=2ln x-ln d at an intersection. M1: Uses the logarithm power rule to write 2ln x=ln(x^2). M1: Uses logarithm product or quotient rules to combine the logarithms. A1: Obtains x^2-2dx+9d=0.

parts.label: b.ii
parts.scheme: A1: Forms the discriminant (-2d)^2-4(1)(9d). M1: Uses the two-distinct-intersections condition to require the discriminant to be positive. A1: Simplifies the discriminant condition to d^2-9d>0.

parts.label: b.iii
parts.text: Find the range of possible values of d.
parts.scheme: M1: Solves d(d-9)>0 by a sign test, graph, or equivalent inequality method. A1: Uses d>0 to obtain d>9.

parts.label: c
parts.text: For d=10, find q-p in the form a sqrt(b).
parts.scheme: A1: Substitutes d=10 to obtain x^2-20x+90=0. M1: Attempts to solve the three-term quadratic equation. A1: Obtains p=10-sqrt(10) and q=10+sqrt(10). M1: Subtracts the two x-values in the correct order q-p. A1: Obtains q-p=2sqrt(10).

solution.outline: The vertical asymptote is x=0. The two-intersection condition gives d>9. For d=10, p=10-sqrt(10), q=10+sqrt(10), so q-p=2sqrt(10).

text: For f(x)=e^(cos 2x) on -pi/4<=x<=5pi/4, find and classify the stationary points, sketch the curve on 0<=x<=pi using second-derivative information, derive the required Maclaurin expansions through x^4, and use the first two non-zero terms to approximate the stated definite integral.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the coordinates where the gradient is zero.
parts.scheme: M1: Attempts the chain rule to differentiate e^(cos 2x). A1: Obtains f'(x)=-2sin(2x)e^(cos 2x). M1: Sets sin(2x)=0 to find stationary abscissae. A1: Obtains x=0, pi/2 and pi in the required interval. A1: Obtains the coordinates (0,e), (pi/2,1/e) and (pi,e).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use second derivatives to classify the two maxima and one minimum.
parts.scheme: M1: Differentiates f' using the product rule. A1: Obtains the correct second derivative expression. R1: Uses f''(0)=f''(pi)=-4e<0 to identify both local maxima. R1: Uses f''(pi/2)=4/e>0 to identify the local minimum.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sketch the curve on 0<=x<=pi with the relative curvature shown.
parts.scheme: A1: Draws the correct general curve shape on 0<=x<=pi. A1: Shows maxima at (0,e) and (pi,e) and the minimum at (pi/2,1/e). A1: Shows the greater rate of gradient change at the maxima than at the minimum.

parts.label: d.i
parts.text: Find the Maclaurin series for cos(2x) through x^4.
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes 2x into the cosine Maclaurin series through the fourth-power term. A1: Obtains cos(2x)=1-2x^2+(2/3)x^4+... .

parts.label: d.ii
parts.text: Find the Maclaurin series for e^(cos(2x)-1) through x^4.
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes the series for cos(2x)-1 into the exponential Maclaurin series, or uses an equivalent product of exponential series. A1: Retains all contributions through x^4, including the squared x^2 term. A1: Obtains e^(cos(2x)-1)=1-2x^2+(8/3)x^4+... .

parts.label: d.iii
parts.text: Write the Maclaurin series for f through x^4.
parts.scheme: A1: Obtains f(x)=e-2ex^2+(8e/3)x^4+... .

parts.label: e
parts.text: Use the first two non-zero terms to show the stated integral approximation.
parts.scheme: M1: Approximates the integrand by e(1-2x^2) over the stated limits. A1: Integrates to e[x-(2/3)x^3] from 0 to 1/10. A1: Simplifies the approximation to 149e/1500.

solution.outline: The stationary points are (0,e) and (pi,e), both local maxima, and (pi/2,1/e), a local minimum. The series are cos(2x)=1-2x^2+(2/3)x^4+..., e^(cos(2x)-1)=1-2x^2+(8/3)x^4+..., and f(x)=e-2ex^2+(8e/3)x^4+.... The requested integral is approximately 149e/1500.

text: Let f(x)=ln(5x)/(kx), where x>0 and k>0. (a) Show the stated first derivative. (b) Find the x-coordinate of the unique maximum P. (c) Show the stated x-coordinate of the unique inflection point Q. (d) The region under f between P and Q has area 3; find k.

parts.label: a
parts.scheme: M1: Attempts to differentiate using the quotient rule. A1: Substitutes the derivative of ln(5x) correctly into the quotient rule. A1: Simplifies to f'(x)=(1-ln(5x))/(kx^2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the x-coordinate of the maximum point P.
parts.scheme: M1: Sets f'(x)=0. A1: Obtains ln(5x)=1. A1: Obtains x=e/5.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the x-coordinate of the inflection point Q is e^(3/2)/5.
parts.scheme: M1: Sets f''(x)=0 to locate the inflection point. A1: Obtains ln(5x)=3/2. A1: Obtains x=e^(3/2)/5.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Given that the enclosed area is 3, find k.
parts.scheme: M1: Attempts the required definite integral for the area. A1: Uses u=ln(5x) with du/dx=1/x. A1: Obtains the antiderivative (ln(5x))^2/(2k). A1: Uses the correct limits e/5 and e^(3/2)/5. A1: Evaluates the area as 5/(8k). M1: Sets 5/(8k)=3. A1: Obtains k=5/24.

solution.outline: P has x-coordinate e/5, Q has x-coordinate e^(3/2)/5, and k=5/24.

text: (a) Express -3+sqrt(3)i in polar exponential form. Let u, v and w be the roots of z^3=-3+sqrt(3)i. (b) Find the three roots in polar exponential form. (c) Find the area of triangle UVW on an Argand diagram. (d) Use the sum of the roots to prove the stated cosine identity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express -3+sqrt(3)i in the form r e^(i theta).
parts.scheme: M1: Attempts to find the modulus. A1: Obtains r=sqrt(12)=2sqrt(3). M1: Attempts to find the argument in the correct quadrant. A1: Forms a correct argument calculation for the second quadrant. A1: Obtains theta=5pi/6 and the correct exponential form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the three cube roots in polar exponential form.
parts.scheme: M1: Attempts to find a cube root using de Moivre's theorem. A1: Obtains the root 12^(1/6)e^(5pi i/18). M1: Attempts to find the other roots by changing the argument by 2pi/3. A1: Obtains the root 12^(1/6)e^(-7pi i/18). A1: Obtains the root 12^(1/6)e^(17pi i/18).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the area of triangle UVW on the Argand diagram.
parts.scheme: M1: Attempts to decompose UVW into three congruent triangles with the origin. A1: Uses two radii of length 12^(1/6) in the triangle-area formula. A1: Uses the included angle 2pi/3. A1: Obtains the area (3sqrt(3)/4)12^(1/3).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use the sum of the roots to prove the stated cosine identity.
parts.scheme: R1: States that u+v+w=0. A1: Substitutes the three roots into the sum. M1: Takes the real parts of the complex-number equation. A1: Uses cos(-7pi/18)=cos(7pi/18) to obtain the required identity.

solution.outline: -3+sqrt(3)i=2sqrt(3)e^(5pi i/6); the roots have arguments 5pi/18, -7pi/18 and 17pi/18 with modulus 12^(1/6); triangle area is (3sqrt(3)/4)12^(1/3); the real parts of u+v+w=0 give the required cosine identity.

text: Let f(x)=e^(sin x). (a) Find its first two derivatives and its Maclaurin series through x^2. (b) Show that the coefficient of x^3 is zero. (c) Use the Maclaurin series for arctan x and e^(3x)-1 to find the series for arctan(e^(3x)-1) through x^3. (d) Find the stated limit as x tends to zero.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the first two derivatives and the Maclaurin series of f through x^2.
parts.scheme: M1: Attempts to use the chain rule for the first derivative. A1: Obtains f'(x)=cos(x)e^(sin x). M1: Attempts to use the product rule for the second derivative. A1: Obtains f''(x)=e^(sin x)(cos^2(x)-sin(x)). M1: Attempts to find f(0), f'(0) and f''(0). A1: Obtains f(0)=f'(0)=f''(0)=1. M1: Substitutes the derivative values into the Maclaurin formula. A1: Obtains f(x)=1+x+x^2/2 through the x^2 term.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the coefficient of x^3 in the Maclaurin series for f is zero.
parts.scheme: M1: Attempts to differentiate f''(x). A1: Applies the product and chain rules to form the derivative of e^(sin x)(cos^2(x)-sin(x)). A1: Obtains a correct expression for f'''(x). M1: Substitutes x=0 and obtains f'''(0)=0, so the x^3 coefficient is zero.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the Maclaurin series for arctan(e^(3x)-1) through x^3.
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes 3x into the Maclaurin series for e^x. A1: Obtains the expansion of e^(3x) through x^3. M1: Substitutes e^(3x)-1 into the Maclaurin series for arctan x. A1: Forms the correct composed series before collecting terms. M1: Selects all terms that contribute through degree three. A1: Obtains arctan(e^(3x)-1)=3x+(9/2)x^2-(9/2)x^3 through x^3.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the limit of (f(x)-1)/arctan(e^(3x)-1) as x tends to zero.
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes the two series into the quotient. A1: Cancels the leading factor x and identifies the leading numerator and denominator coefficients. A1: Obtains the limit 1/3.

text: For f(x)=90e^(-0.5x), x>0: (a) find the intersection with y=x; (b) find the exact tangency point Q where the tangent gradient is -1; (c) show the tangent line equation; (d) find its intersection with y=x and the enclosed area A; (e) use the inverse-function symmetry to find the larger shaded area bounded by f, f inverse and the tangent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the x-coordinate where f intersects y=x.
parts.scheme: M1: Attempts to solve 90e^(-0.5x)=x for the graph-line intersection. A1: Obtains x=5.57 to three significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact coordinates of the tangency point Q.
parts.scheme: A1: Differentiates to obtain f'(x)=-45e^(-0.5x). M1: Sets f'(x)=-1 for the required tangent gradient. A1: Obtains the x-coordinate 2ln(45). A1: Obtains the y-coordinate 2 and hence Q=(2ln(45),2).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the tangent line is y=-x+2ln(45)+2.
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes Q into a line of gradient -1. A1: Obtains y=-x+2ln(45)+2.

parts.label: d.i
parts.text: Find the x-coordinate where the tangent intersects y=x.
parts.scheme: A1: Solves the two line equations to obtain x=ln(45)+1.

parts.label: d.ii
parts.text: Find the area A enclosed by f, y=x and the tangent.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses a sum of two integrals of differences between the boundary functions. A1: Forms the correct integral between the two lines with correct limits. A1: Forms the correct integral between f and the tangent with correct limits. A1: Obtains area A=1.52.

text: For f(x)=(3x+2)/(4x^2-1): (a) find excluded values; (b) differentiate; (c) find the inflection x-coordinate; (d) sketch with intercepts, extrema and asymptotes. For g(x)=(4x^2-1)/(3x+2): (e) find all asymptotes; (f) solve f(x)<g(x).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find p and q, the excluded values of f.
parts.scheme: M1: Solves 4x^2-1=0, for example by factorising. A1: Obtains p=1/2 and q=-1/2 in either order.

parts.label: b
parts.scheme: M1: Attempts quotient rule or product rule differentiation. A1: Forms one correct signed numerator contribution with denominator (4x^2-1)^2. A1: Obtains f'(x)=(-12x^2-16x-3)/(4x^2-1)^2 or an equivalent correct form.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the x-coordinate of the inflection point.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses a local minimum of f' or solves f''(x)=0. A1: Obtains x=-1.60.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Sketch f for -3<=x<=3 with intercepts, extrema and asymptotes.
parts.scheme: A1: Shows both vertical asymptotes x=-1/2 and x=1/2. A1: Shows the horizontal asymptote y=0. A1: Shows all three branches with correct asymptotic behaviour. A1: Shows the local maximum (-0.226,-1.66) and local minimum (-1.11,-0.339). A1: Shows the x-intercept -2/3 and y-intercept -2.

parts.label: e
parts.scheme: A1: Obtains the vertical asymptote x=-2/3. A1: Obtains the oblique-asymptote gradient 4/3. M1: Uses an appropriate method, such as polynomial division, to find the complete oblique asymptote. A1: Obtains y=(4/3)x-8/9.

parts.label: f
parts.scheme: M1: Finds at least one critical value for the rational inequality. A1: Obtains -2/3<x<-0.569. A1: Obtains -1/2<x<1/2. A1: Obtains x>1.32.

text: For f'(x)=1/[x(k-x)], k>0: express it in partial fractions and find f(x). A colony with P(0)=1200 obeys dP/dt=P(k-P)/(5k); derive the stated solution, use P(10)=2400 to find k, and find when growth is greatest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find partial-fraction constants a and b.
parts.scheme: A1: Forms 1/[x(k-x)]=a/x+b/(k-x) and clears denominators. M1: Compares coefficients or substitutes x=0 and x=k. A1: Obtains a=b=1/k.

parts.label: b
parts.scheme: M1: Attempts to integrate the partial-fraction expression. A1A1: Obtains f(x)=(1/k)(ln|x|-ln|k-x|)+c, awarding one mark for each logarithmic term.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Solve the differential equation to show the stated expression for P.
parts.scheme: M1: Separates variables and integrates both sides. A1: Obtains an equivalent logarithmic relation after integration. M1: Substitutes t=0 and P=1200 to determine the integration constant, or uses the equivalent exponential form. A1: Obtains the corresponding constant relation from the initial condition. A1: Forms the exponential relation involving P/(k-P). M1: Attempts to rearrange the relation and isolate P. A1: Obtains an equivalent isolated expression for P. AG: Shows P=1200k/((k-1200)e^(-t/5)+1200).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find k to four significant figures.
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes t=10 and P=2400 into the derived model. A1: Forms the resulting equation in k. A1: Obtains k=2845 to four significant figures.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the time when dP/dt is maximum.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the maximum of dP/dt, a zero of the second derivative, or P=k/2. A2: Obtains t=1.58 days (values rounding to 1.6 are accepted).

solution.outline: a=b=1/k; f(x)=(1/k)(ln|x|-ln|k-x|)+c; P=1200k/((k-1200)e^(-t/5)+1200); k=2845; the maximum rate occurs at t=1.58 days.

text: Flight time T is normal with mean 75 and standard deviation sigma. Given P(T>82)=0.02: find sigma, P(T>80), conditional probability P(T<82 given T>80), expected count above 80 among 64 flights, and probability more than 6 are above 80.

parts.label: a
parts.scheme: M1: Uses inverse normal for the 98th percentile to obtain z=2.0537... A1: Forms 2.0537...=(82-75)/sigma. A1: Obtains sigma=3.41.

parts.label: b
parts.scheme: M1: Identifies the correct upper-tail normal area for T>80. A1: Obtains P(T>80)=0.0712.

parts.label: c
parts.scheme: M1: Recognizes the required numerator P(80<T<82). M1: Uses P(T<82 given T>80)=P(80<T<82)/P(T>80). A1: Obtains the numerator 0.051193... A1: Obtains 0.719.

parts.text: Find expected count above 80 among 64 flights.
parts.scheme: M1: Models the count as B(64,0.071193...). A1: Uses E(X)=64 times 0.071193... A1: Obtains E(X)=4.56 flights.

parts.label: e
parts.scheme: M1: Uses P(X>6)=1-P(X<=6) for the binomial model. A1: Obtains 1-0.83088... A1: Obtains 0.169.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

parts.label: c.i

parts.label: c.ii

parts.label: d.i

parts.scheme: M1: Chooses to sketch f' or f'' and differentiates by quotient or product rule. text: f(x)=arcsin((x^2-1)/(x^2+1)); g is f restricted to x>=0. Establish parity, asymptote, derivative and monotonicity, then find and graph g inverse.

parts.label: a
parts.scheme: R1: Shows f(-x)=f(x), hence f is even.

parts.label: b
parts.scheme: A1: Uses x tending to plus or minus infinity to obtain arcsin(1)=pi/2. A1: States horizontal asymptote y=pi/2.

parts.label: c.i
parts.scheme: M1: Attempts quotient-rule differentiation of (x^2-1)/(x^2+1). A1: Obtains derivative 4x/(x^2+1)^2 for the inner rational function. M1: Applies the chain rule for arcsin. M1: Forms the arcsin derivative expression with sqrt(1-u^2). A1: Simplifies the radical using (x^2+1)^2-(x^2-1)^2=4x^2. A1: Obtains f'(x)=2x/(sqrt(x^2)(x^2+1)).

parts.label: c.ii
parts.scheme: A1: Uses sqrt(x^2)=|x| and |x|=-x for x<0. A1: Obtains f'(x)=-2/(x^2+1), or correctly establishes negative numerator and positive denominator. R1: Concludes f'(x)<0 and f decreases for x<0.

parts.label: d
parts.scheme: M1: Sets x=arcsin((y^2-1)/(y^2+1)) for inversion. A1: Uses sin x=(y^2-1)/(y^2+1) and rearranges to y^2=(1+sin x)/(1-sin x). A1: Recognizes the positive root because the domain of g is x>=0. A1: Obtains g^(-1)(x)=sqrt((1+sin x)/(1-sin x)). A1: Justifies the branch/range choice consistently with g restricted to nonnegative inputs.

parts.label: e
parts.scheme: A1: States -pi/2<=x<pi/2.

parts.label: f
parts.scheme: A1: Sketch has correct domain/range and y-intercept (0,1). A1: Shows asymptotic behavior as x approaches pi/2. A1: Labels vertical asymptote x=pi/2.

solution.outline: f is even; asymptote y=pi/2; f'(x)=2x/(sqrt(x^2)(x^2+1)); g^(-1)(x)=sqrt((1+sin x)/(1-sin x)) on [-pi/2,pi/2), with vertical asymptote x=pi/2.

text: For f(x)=sqrt(x^2-1), 1<=x<=2, sketch f; find its inverse and inverse domain/range; rotate about the y-axis to derive container volume V=pi(h^3/3+h), maximum volume, filling time at 0.4 m^3 s^-1, and height rate at half capacity.

parts.label: c.ii
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes the maximum height h=sqrt(3) into V. A1: Obtains maximum volume 2sqrt(3)pi m^3, approximately 10.9 m^3.

text: Chocolate muffin weight C is N(62,2.9) and banana muffin weight B is N(68,3.4); 60% are chocolate. Find normal and binomial probabilities, total and conditional probabilities below 61 g, then find adjusted chocolate standard deviation sigma when the mixed probability below 61 g is 0.157.

parts.label: a
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the normal distribution C~N(62,2.9^2) to evaluate P(C<61). A1: Obtains P(C<61)=0.365.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For 12 chocolate muffins, find the probability exactly 5 weigh less than 61 g.
parts.scheme: M1: Models the number below 61 g as X~B(12,0.365...). A1: Obtains P(X=5)=0.214.

parts.label: c.i
parts.text: Find the probability a randomly selected muffin weighs less than 61 g.
parts.scheme: A1: Obtains P(B<61)=0.0197555... from the banana normal distribution. M1: Forms the total-probability expression 0.6P(C<61)+0.4P(B<61), or equivalent tree reasoning. A1: Substitutes the two component probabilities into the total-probability expression. A1: Obtains the overall probability 0.227.

parts.label: c.ii
parts.text: Given it weighs less than 61 g, find the probability it is chocolate.
parts.scheme: M1: Recognizes and sets up conditional probability for chocolate given weight below 61 g. A1: Forms (0.6 times 0.365112...)/0.226969... . A1: Obtains the conditional probability 0.965.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the adjusted standard deviation sigma.
parts.scheme: M1: Forms 0.6P(C<61)+0.4P(B<61)=0.157 for the adjusted chocolate distribution. A1: Obtains P(C<61)=0.248496... for the adjusted chocolate distribution. M1: Uses inverse normal, a valid graph/table, or an equivalent method to determine the corresponding standardized value. A1: Forms (61-62)/sigma=-0.679229... or an equivalent correct substitution. A1: Obtains sigma=1.47 g.

solution.outline: P(C<61)=0.365; P(X=5)=0.214; overall P(weight<61)=0.227; P(chocolate | weight<61)=0.965; adjusted sigma=1.47 g.

text: Two airplanes have position vectors r_A=(19,-1,1)+t(-6,2,4) and r_B=(1,0,12)+t(4,2,-2), where 0<=t<=2.5 minutes. Determine a bearing, compare speeds, find the acute angle and crossing point, then minimize their simultaneous separation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the three-figure bearing on which airplane B is travelling.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the horizontal direction components of B to form the bearing angle, for example 90 degrees-arctan(1/2). A1: Gives the three-figure bearing 063 degrees.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that airplane A travels at a greater speed than airplane B.
parts.scheme: M1: Finds the magnitude of at least one direction vector as a speed. A1: Obtains speeds sqrt(56)=7.48... and sqrt(24)=4.89... km min^-1 and concludes A is faster.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the acute angle between the airplanes' lines of flight.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the angle-between-direction-vectors formula. A1: Obtains cos(theta)=-0.7637...=-7/sqrt(84), or an equivalent correct dot-product evaluation. M1: Uses 180 degrees-theta to obtain the acute angle. A1: Obtains the acute angle 40.2 degrees.

parts.label: d.i
parts.text: Find the coordinates of their crossing point P.
parts.scheme: M1: Sets r_A(t_1)=r_B(t_2) and forms at least two coordinate equations using separate time parameters. M1: Attempts to solve the resulting simultaneous equations for t_1 or t_2. A1: Obtains t_1=2 or t_2=3/2. M1: Substitutes the relevant time into r_A or r_B. A1: Obtains P=(7,3,9).

parts.label: d.ii
parts.text: Find the time between the airplanes arriving at P.
parts.scheme: M1: Forms the difference t_1-t_2. A1: Obtains 0.5 minutes, equivalently 30 seconds.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the minimum value of the simultaneous distance D(t) between the airplanes.
parts.scheme: M1: Forms r_B-r_A or r_A-r_B using the same time parameter. M1: Forms D(t)=sqrt((10t-18)^2+1+(11-6t)^2), or an equivalent expression. A1: Gives a correct distance function D(t). M1: Finds a local minimum of D(t), or equivalently solves D'(t)=0. A1: Obtains t=123/68=1.8088... and the minimum distance sqrt(1190)/34=1.01 km.

solution.outline: Bearing of B=063 degrees; speeds are sqrt(56) and sqrt(24) km min^-1, so A is faster; acute angle=40.2 degrees; P=(7,3,9), reached 0.5 minutes apart; min D(t)=sqrt(1190)/34=1.01 km at t=123/68.

text: A marsupial population satisfies dP/dt=kP(1-P/N), where k,N>0. Interpret the rate, derive its second derivative, establish the maximum population growth rate, solve the logistic equation with P(0)=P_0, and determine k given P(10)=3P_0 and N=4P_0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Interpret dP/dt in the population model.
parts.scheme: A1: Interprets dP/dt as the instantaneous rate of growth or change of the marsupial population with respect to time.

parts.label: b
parts.scheme: M1: Implicitly differentiates the logistic equation, either after expanding or by the product rule. A2: Obtains the correct differentiated expression before substitution, including the factor 1-2P/N or an algebraically equivalent form. A1: Substitutes dP/dt=kP(1-P/N) to obtain d^2P/dt^2=k^2P(1-P/N)(1-2P/N).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show population growth is maximized when P=N/2 and justify the result.
parts.scheme: M1: Sets d^2P/dt^2=0. A2: Obtains the stationary population values P=0, N/2, N, including P=N/2. M1: Uses concavity or the first derivative to identify the local maximum at P=N/2. R1: Provides a valid justification, such as a labelled sign diagram, a labelled sketch, or correct second-derivative signs on either side of P=N/2.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the maximum value of dP/dt.
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes P=N/2 into dP/dt=kP(1-P/N). A1: Obtains the maximum rate kN/4.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Solve the logistic differential equation to obtain the stated logarithmic solution.
parts.scheme: M1: Separates variables into an integral in P and an integral in t. M1: Attempts to express the separated rational function in partial fractions. A1: Obtains a correct partial-fractions decomposition, for example N/[P(N-P)]=1/P+1/(N-P). A2: Integrates to obtain ln P-ln(N-P)=kt+C, or an algebraically equivalent logarithmic form. M1: Uses t=0 and P=P_0 to determine the integration constant in terms of N and P_0. A1: Obtains kt=ln[(P/P_0)((N-P_0)/(N-P))].

parts.label: f
parts.text: Find k given P(10)=3P_0 and N=4P_0.
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes t=10, P=3P_0, and N=4P_0 into the derived logarithmic solution. A1: Obtains k=ln(9)/10=ln(3)/5=0.220.

solution.outline: dP/dt is the instantaneous population growth rate. d^2P/dt^2=k^2P(1-P/N)(1-2P/N); growth is greatest at P=N/2, where dP/dt=kN/4. The solution is kt=ln[(P/P_0)((N-P_0)/(N-P))]. Under the given data k=ln(9)/10=ln(3)/5=0.220.

parts.scheme: M1: Correctly substitutes x=78 into the student's regression equation. A1: Obtains 81.3930... and predicts 81 to the nearest integer.

text: Employee working time T is normally distributed with mean 42 and standard deviation 10.7. Find selected normal, independent-event, conditional-probability, binomial, and inverse-normal results for the stated work-time events.

parts.label: a
parts.scheme: M1: Recognizes the required normal probability P(T>40). A1: Obtains P(T>40)=0.574136..., giving 0.574.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the fourth of four employees is the only one working more than 40 hours.
parts.scheme: M1: Multiplies four independent probabilities using P(T>40) and P(T<40). A1: Forms (1-p)^3p with p=P(T>40). A1: Obtains 0.0443430..., giving 0.0443.

parts.label: c.i
parts.text: Given T>40, find the probability that T<55.
parts.scheme: M1: Recognizes the conditional probability P(T<55 | T>40). A1: Forms P(40<T<55)/P(T>40). A1: Obtains the numerator 0.461944... and denominator 0.574136... . A1: Obtains P(T<55 | T>40)=0.804590..., giving 0.805.

parts.label: c.ii
parts.text: For ten such employees, find the probability that exactly five work less than 55 hours.
parts.scheme: M1: Recognizes a binomial probability model. A1: Sets X~B(10,0.804589...). A1: Obtains P(X=5)=0.024211..., giving 0.0242.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the largest part-time work time a under the stated probability conditions.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses that the three probability regions sum to 1. M1: Expresses the regions using x=P(T<a), for example x+0.904+2x=1. A1: Obtains P(T<a)=0.032. A1: Uses the normal distribution to obtain a=22.18167..., giving 22.2 hours (22.1 accepted).

solution.outline: P(T>40)=0.574; fourth-only probability=0.0443; P(T<55 | T>40)=0.805; P(exactly five of ten)=0.0242; maximum part-time threshold a=22.2 hours.

text: For A=(1,2,3), B=(k,-2,1), C=(5,0,2), derive vectors and collinearity, give the line through the points for k=9 and show it is skew to a second line, then for k not equal to 9 determine the containing plane and its point closest to the origin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down vectors AB and AC.
parts.scheme: A1: Obtains AB=(k-1,-4,-2). A1: Obtains AC=(4,-2,-1).

parts.label: b
parts.scheme: M1: Uses proportional direction components, for example k-1=2 times 4, to establish k=9.

parts.label: c.i
parts.text: For k=9, find a vector equation of L1.
parts.scheme: M1: Forms a line equation from a point, parameter and direction vector. A1: Obtains L1: r=(1,2,3)+lambda(4,-2,-1).

parts.label: c.ii
parts.text: Show L1 and L2 are skew.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses a separate parameter mu for L2. A1: Obtains L2: r=(1,0,1)+mu(2,3,-1). A1: Equates coordinates to form at least two equations, such as 1+4lambda=1+2mu and 2-2lambda=3mu. M1: Attempts to solve two simultaneous equations in lambda and mu. A1: Obtains a valid parameter pair from two equations, for example lambda=0.25 and mu=0.5. M1: Tests the remaining coordinate equation. R1: Obtains a valid contradiction, so the lines do not intersect. R1: Shows the direction vectors are not parallel and concludes the non-intersecting lines are skew.

parts.label: d.i
parts.text: For k not equal to 9, find the Cartesian equation of plane Pi.
parts.scheme: M1: Finds a normal vector using a cross product of two in-plane vectors. A1: Obtains AB cross AC=(k-9)(0,1,-2), or an equivalent normal vector. M1: Substitutes a normal vector and an in-plane point into a plane equation. A1: Obtains the Cartesian equation y-2z=-4 (k not equal to 9).

parts.label: d.ii
parts.text: Find the point on Pi closest to the origin.
parts.scheme: M1: Forms the line through the origin perpendicular to Pi, with direction (0,1,-2). A1: Writes the perpendicular line r=t(0,1,-2). M1: Substitutes the perpendicular line into the plane to find its intersection point. A1: Obtains t=-4/5. A1: Obtains the closest point (0,-0.8,1.6).

solution.outline: AB=(k-1,-4,-2), AC=(4,-2,-1), and k=9. L1: r=(1,2,3)+lambda(4,-2,-1); it is skew to L2. For k not equal to 9, Pi is y-2z=-4 and its closest point to the origin is (0,-0.8,1.6).

text: Prove by contradiction that p^2-8q-11 is not equal to zero for any integers p and q.

parts.label: main
parts.text: Prove the stated result by contradiction.
parts.scheme: M1: Assumes p^2-8q-11=0 for integers p and q. R1: Uses p^2=8q+11=2(4q+5)+1 to conclude that p is odd, or gives an equivalent valid parity argument. M1: Sets p=2k+1 for an integer k. A1: Substitutes and expands to obtain 4k^2+4k+1=8q+11. A1: Rearranges to 2k^2+2k=4q+5, or an equivalent equality with one side even and the other odd. R1: States the contradiction that the left side is even while the right side is odd, and therefore the assumed equality is impossible.

solution.outline: Assuming equality forces p to be odd and then yields 2k^2+2k=4q+5, an even-equals-odd contradiction. Thus p^2-8q-11 is never zero for integer p,q.

text: A 45 cm by 600 cm sheet forms an open gutter with two vertical 10 cm sides and a circular arc of radius 12 cm. With central angle theta, find theta and cross-sectional area. With inflow rate R'(t)=50cos(2pi t/5)+3000, determine whether 60-second rainfall overflows the gutter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show theta=2.08 radians, correct to three significant figures.
parts.scheme: M1: Recognizes 45=10+10+arc length. A1: Obtains arc length 25 cm. A1: Uses 25=12theta to obtain theta=2.08 radians to three significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the gutter cross-section.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the cosine rule, sine rule, or equivalent right-triangle trigonometry to determine the chord width. A1: Forms w^2=12^2+12^2-2(12)(12)cos(2.08), or an equivalent relation. A1: Obtains w=20.6977..., equivalently w/2=10.3488... . M1: Forms the circular segment area as sector OAB minus triangle OAB. A1: Obtains segment area 0.5(12^2)(2.08)-0.5(12^2)sin(2.08)=86.8944... . M1: Uses a valid decomposition for the total cross-sectional area, for example segment plus rectangle of area 10w. A1: Obtains cross-sectional area 293.871..., giving 294 cm^2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine with justification whether the gutter overflowed.
parts.scheme: A1: Computes gutter volume as 600 times the cross-sectional area, obtaining 176323 cm^3 (or 176658 cm^3 from the exact area). M1: Recognizes that entering rainfall over 60 seconds is represented by integral from 0 to 60 of R'(t) dt. A1: Evaluates the definite integral using an antiderivative, including (250/(2pi))sin(2pi times 60/5)+3000 times 60. A1: Obtains rainfall volume 180000 cm^3 over 60 seconds. A1: Concludes that the gutter overflows because rainfall volume exceeds gutter volume.

solution.outline: theta=2.08 radians; cross-sectional area=294 cm^2; gutter volume is about 176323 cm^3 while 60-second rainfall is 180000 cm^3, so it overflows.

text: X has density f(x)=6/(pi sqrt(16-x^2)) for 0 less than or equal to x less than or equal to 2. Find its expectation and a probability, then apply these results to independent success trials, binomial probabilities, and consecutive-success arrangements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the exact value of E(X).
parts.scheme: A1: Forms E(X)=integral from 0 to 2 of 6x/(pi sqrt(16-x^2)) dx. M1: Attempts integration by inspection or substitution, for example u=16-x^2. A1: Obtains an antiderivative equivalent to -6/pi times sqrt(16-x^2). M1: Attempts to substitute the definite-integral limits and evaluate. A1: Obtains E(X)=24/pi-6sqrt(12)/pi=12(2-sqrt(3))/pi.

parts.label: b
parts.scheme: M1: Forms P(X<0.5)=integral from 0 to 0.5 of f(x) dx. A1: Obtains P(X<0.5)=0.239358..., giving 0.239.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the least trials for 99 percent certainty of at least one success.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses P(at least one success)=1-P(no successes) after n independent trials. A1: Forms 1-(1-0.239...)^n greater than or equal to 0.99, or an equivalent binomial approach. A1: Obtains the least required number as 17 trials.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the probability that exactly three of ten trials succeed.
parts.scheme: M1: Recognizes a binomial model B(10,0.239...). A1: Obtains P(Y=3)=0.242430..., giving 0.242.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Write the number of consecutive arrangements for three successes in ten trials.
parts.scheme: A1: Obtains 8 consecutive placements for three successes in ten trials.

parts.label: f.i
parts.text: Write the number of consecutive arrangements for three successes in n trials.
parts.scheme: A1: Obtains n-2 possible consecutive placements.

parts.label: f.ii
parts.text: Find the greatest n for which the conditional probability of three consecutive successes exceeds 0.05.
parts.scheme: A1: Obtains nC3 as the number of ways to place three successes in n trials. A1: Forms the conditional probability (n-2)/(nC3). M1: Attempts to solve (n-2)/(nC3)>0.05, equivalently 6/[n(n-1)]>0.05. A1: Finds the boundary, for example n=11 gives 0.054545... while n=12 gives 0.0454545... . A1: Obtains the greatest value n=11.

solution.outline: E(X)=12(2-sqrt(3))/pi; P(X<0.5)=0.239; least trials=17; P(exactly three of ten)=0.242; consecutive placements are 8 for ten trials and n-2 for n trials; greatest n is 11.

text: For two draws without replacement from r red and y yellow balls with P(YY)=1/3, derive and solve the quadratic in y and give two positive integer pairs. Then with 10 red and y yellow balls, find P(YYY), and find y when adding one yellow ball doubles this probability.

parts.label: a
parts.scheme: M1: Forms a two-factor yellow numerator and two-factor total denominator for P(YY). A1: Obtains y(y-1)/[(r+y)(r+y-1)]=1/3. M1: Clears fractions and expands brackets. A1: Obtains 3y^2-3y=y^2+2ry-y+r^2-r, leading to 2y^2-2(r+1)y+r-r^2=0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve for y in terms of r.
parts.scheme: M1: Applies the quadratic formula to solve for y. A1: Obtains y=[2(r+1) plus or minus sqrt(4(r+1)^2-8(r-r^2))]/4. A1: Simplifies to y=[2(r+1) plus or minus sqrt(12r^2+4)]/4. R1: Rejects the negative root because ball counts are positive, yielding y=[(r+1)+sqrt(3r^2+1)]/2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find two positive integer pairs r,y.
parts.scheme: M1: Attempts to find positive integer pairs, for example by table or substitution. A1: Finds one valid pair, such as (r,y)=(1,2). A2: Finds a second valid pair, such as (r,y)=(4,6).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find P(YYY) in terms of y.
parts.scheme: M1: Forms the without-replacement three-draw probability with three y factors and total factors including y+10. A1: Obtains the numerator y(y-1)(y-2). A1: Obtains denominator (y+10)(y+9)(y+8).

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the initial number of yellow balls.

text: For dy/dx=(x^2+3y^2)/(xy), x,y>0 and y(1)=2, use Euler's method, solve the differential equation, compare concavity, locate an inflexion by derivative graph, and use the given second derivative to find the positive line y=mx through the inflexion.

parts.label: a
parts.scheme: M1: Uses Euler recurrence y1=y0+h f(x0,y0). A1: Obtains y1=2+0.1[1^2+3(2)^2]/2=2.65.

parts.label: b
parts.scheme: M1: Uses homogeneous substitution y=vx. A1: Differentiates to dy/dx=v+x dv/dx. M1: Substitutes and obtains a relation equivalent to x dv/dx=(1+2v^2)/v. A1: Obtains x dv/dx=(1+2v^2)/v. text: A circle has centre O and radius 4 cm. Chord AB has length 5 cm and angle AOB=theta. Find theta in radians and the area of the shaded major sector.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the value of theta, giving the answer in radians.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the cosine rule in triangle AOB, or splits it into two congruent right triangles. A1: Obtains cos(theta)=(4^2+4^2-5^2)/(2*4*4), or equivalently sin(theta/2)=2.5/4. A1: Obtains theta=1.35 radians.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the shaded region.
parts.scheme: M1: Sets up the area of the shaded major sector. A1: Uses (1/2)*4*4*(2*pi-1.35...), or an equivalent expression. A1: Obtains the shaded area as 39.5 cm^2.

solution.outline: theta=1.35 radians; shaded area=39.5 cm^2.

text: On 1 January 2020, Laurie invests P in an account paying a nominal annual interest rate of 5.5%, compounded quarterly. The end-of-year amount follows a geometric sequence with common ratio r.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find r, giving the answer to four significant figures.
parts.scheme: M1: Sets up the effective one-year compound-interest multiplier. A1: Uses r=(1+5.5/(4*100))^4. A1: Obtains r=1.056 to four significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the year in which the amount becomes double the amount invested.
parts.scheme: M1: Sets the accumulated value equal to 2P, or enters the equivalent financial-calculator values. A1: Uses 2P=P*(1+5.5/(100*4))^(4n), or 2P=P*(their r)^m, with valid substitution. A1: Obtains 12.7 years and concludes that the amount doubles during 2032.

solution.outline: r=1.056; the investment doubles after 12.7 years, during 2032.

text: A biased six-sided die has P(six)=7/10 and is tossed five times. Find the probability of at most three sixes and of the third six occurring on the fifth toss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability of at most three sixes.
parts.scheme: M1: Recognizes X as a binomial random variable with X~B(5,0.7). M1: Sets up or evaluates P(X<=3). A1: Obtains P(X<=3)=0.472, accepting 0.47178.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the third six is on the fifth toss.
parts.scheme: M1: Recognizes that exactly two sixes must occur in the first four tosses. A1: Uses C(4,2)*(0.7)^2*(0.3)^2*0.7, or the equivalent 0.2646*0.7. A1: Obtains probability 0.185, accepting 0.18522.

parts.text: Find the set of m values for which the two graphs have no intersection points.

text: Seashell length X is normally distributed with mean 25 and unknown variance. P(X<24.15)=0.1446. Determine central/upper-tail probabilities, sigma, binomial counts among 10 shells, and a conditional probability.

parts.label: a
parts.scheme: M1: Uses symmetry of the normal curve, for example 0.5-0.1446. A1: Obtains P(24.15<X<25)=0.3554.

parts.label: b(i)
parts.text: Find the standard deviation sigma of X.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses inverse normal to obtain z=-1.0598. A1: Substitutes (24.15-25)/sigma=-1.0598. A1: Obtains sigma=0.802.

parts.label: b(ii)
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the normal distribution with the derived standard deviation to evaluate the upper tail at 26. A1: Obtains P(X>26)=0.106.

parts.label: c
parts.text: For a sample of 10, find E(Y), where Y counts lengths greater than 26 mm.
parts.scheme: M1: Recognizes Y as a binomial count with n=10 and p=P(X>26). A1: Uses E(Y)=10*0.10621. A1: Obtains E(Y)=1.06.

parts.label: d
parts.scheme: M1: Sets up P(Y=3) using the established binomial distribution. A1: Obtains P(Y=3)=0.0655.

parts.label: e
parts.scheme: M1: Recognizes the required probability as conditional probability given X<26. A1: Uses 0.3554/(1-0.10621). A1: Obtains 0.398.

text: A salt-water tank model satisfies dx/dt=10e^(-t/4)-x/(t+1), with x(0)=0. Establish an integrating factor, solve, analyze the graph, find steepest decrease, and calculate salt leaving in 60 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that t+1 is an integrating factor.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the integrating-factor method or product-rule differentiation of x(t+1). A1: Obtains integrating factor t+1 and verifies the transformed derivative.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve the differential equation and show the stated expression for x(t).
parts.scheme: M1: Multiplies by t+1 and rearranges the differential equation. A1: Obtains (t+1)dx/dt+x=10(t+1)e^(-t/4). A1: Writes d(x(t+1))/dt=10(t+1)e^(-t/4) and integrates. M1: Attempts integration by parts on the right-hand side. A1: Obtains -40(t+1)e^(-t/4)-160e^(-t/4)+C. M1: Uses x(0)=0 to determine the constant, or factors the exponential expression equivalently. A1: Obtains C=200 and the equivalent expression before final simplification. A1: Obtains x(t)=(200-40e^(-t/4)(t+5))/(t+1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sketch x against t for 0<=t<=60 and find the maximum amount and time.
parts.scheme: A1: Sketch starts at the origin and has a local maximum over 0<=t<=60. A1: Sketch has correct concavity over 0<=t<=60. A1: Obtains maximum amount 14.6 grams. A1: Obtains the maximum at t=6.60 minutes. A1: Presents the maximum graph/result consistently with the solved model.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find when the salt amount is decreasing most rapidly.
parts.scheme: M1: Uses an appropriate graph or derivative equation to locate the minimum rate of change. A1: Obtains t=12.9 minutes.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the amount of salt leaving during the first 60 minutes.
parts.scheme: M1: Forms an integral for salt leaving, or incoming salt integral minus x(60). A1: Uses integral_0^60 x(t)/(t+1) dt, or the equivalent conservation expression. A1: Substitutes the solved model into the integral or equivalent expression correctly. A1: Obtains 36.7 grams.

solution.outline: x(t)=(200-40e^(-t/4)(t+5))/(t+1); maximum 14.6 g at t=6.60 min; steepest decrease at t=12.9 min; salt leaving in 60 min=36.7 g.

text: Establish a cotangent double-angle identity, connect tan(theta) and -cot(theta) to a quadratic, then derive exact values for tan(pi/12) and tan(pi/24)-cot(pi/24).

parts.label: a
parts.scheme: M1: States cot(2theta)=1/tan(2theta) and the tangent double-angle identity.

parts.label: b
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes x=tan(theta) and uses part (a), or applies equivalent root relationships. A1: Forms the correct left-hand-side expression for x=tan(theta). A1: Simplifies the x=tan(theta) substitution to zero. M1: Substitutes x=-cot(theta) and uses part (a), or sets up the equivalent second-root calculation. A1: Forms the correct left-hand-side expression for x=-cot(theta). A1: Simplifies the x=-cot(theta) substitution to zero. A1: Clearly establishes both stated values as roots of the given quadratic.

parts.label: c
parts.scheme: M1: Uses part (b) with theta=pi/12, or substitutes theta=pi/12 into tan(2theta). A1: Obtains x^2+2sqrt(3)x-1=0. M1: Attempts to solve the resulting quadratic. A1: Obtains roots -sqrt(3)+/-2. A1: Selects the positive root and obtains tan(pi/12)=2-sqrt(3).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find tan(pi/24)-cot(pi/24) in the form a+b sqrt(3).
parts.scheme: M1: Recognizes the target as the sum of roots for x^2+(2cot(pi/12))x-1=0. A1: Uses tan(pi/24)-cot(pi/24)=-2cot(pi/12). A1: Obtains -2/(2-sqrt(3)). M1: Attempts to rationalize the denominator. A1: Obtains the rationalized constant term -4. A1: Obtains the final exact value -4-2sqrt(3).

solution.outline: cot(2theta)=(1-tan^2(theta))/(2tan(theta)); tan(pi/12)=2-sqrt(3); tan(pi/24)-cot(pi/24)=-4-2sqrt(3).

text: Continuous investigation of cubic polynomials f(x)=x^3-3cx+2 and g(x)=x^3-3cx+d, including stationary points and x-intercept conditions.

parts.label: a.i
parts.scheme: A1: Positive cubic with y-intercept 2. A1: Labels local maximum (-1,4). A1: Labels local minimum (1,0).

parts.label: a.ii
parts.scheme: A1: Positive cubic with y-intercept 2. A1: Labels local maximum (-sqrt(2),2+4sqrt(2)). A1: Labels local minimum (sqrt(2),2-4sqrt(2)).

parts.label: c.ii
parts.text: Find c for two stationary points.
parts.scheme: M1: Considers roots of 3x^2-3c=0. A1: c>0.

parts.label: c.iii
parts.text: Find c for no zero gradient.

parts.label: d.i
parts.scheme: M1: Solves f'(x)=0. A1: Obtains x=+-sqrt(c). A1: Obtains local maximum y=2c^(3/2)+2.

parts.label: d.ii
parts.scheme: A1: Obtains local minimum y=-2c^(3/2)+2.

parts.label: e.i
parts.scheme: R1: Uses local-minimum position relative to x-axis. A1: 0<c<1.

parts.label: e.ii
parts.scheme: M1: Sets local minimum equal to zero or uses c=1 graph. A1: c=1.

parts.label: a.i
parts.text: Prove the stated factorization for n=3.
parts.scheme: M1: Expands (omega-1)(omega^2+omega+1) or uses polynomial division. A1: Obtains omega^3-1.

parts.label: a.ii
parts.text: Deduce the sum of the non-real cube roots.
parts.scheme: R1: Uses omega^3=1 and omega is not 1. R1: Deduces omega^2+omega+1=0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show the product of the two distances for n=3.
parts.scheme: M1: Finds either P0P1 or P0P2 by a valid geometric, trigonometric, coordinate, or complex method. A1: Obtains P0P1=sqrt(3). A1: Obtains P0P2=sqrt(3), hence their product is 3.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Deduce the sum of the nontrivial fourth roots.
parts.scheme: A1: Uses z^4-1=(z-1)(z^3+z^2+z+1), or an equivalent root-sum method. R1: Uses omega^4=1 and omega is not 1 to deduce omega^3+omega^2+omega+1=0.

parts.label: d

parts.label: f.i
parts.scheme: A1: Writes P0P2=|1-omega^2|. A1: Writes P0P3=|1-omega^3|.

parts.label: f.ii
parts.scheme: A1: Writes P0P(n-1)=|1-omega^(n-1)|.

parts.label: g.i
parts.text: Factor the root-sum polynomial over the complex numbers.
parts.scheme: M1: Considers z^(n-1)+z^(n-2)+...+z+1=0. A1: Identifies its roots as omega, omega^2, ..., omega^(n-1). A1: Obtains z^(n-1)+...+z+1=(z-omega)(z-omega^2)...(z-omega^(n-1)).

parts.label: g.ii

text: Continuous investigation of the linear system dx/dt=x-y and dy/dt=ax+y for a=0, -1 and -4, leading to first- and second-order differential-equation solutions.

parts.label: a.i
parts.scheme: M1: Separates variables or uses a correct integrating-factor setup for dy/dt=y. A1: Obtains ln(y)=t+c or ln|y|=t+c. A1: Obtains y=Ae^t.

parts.label: a.ii
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes y=Ae^t into dx/dt=x-y.

parts.label: a.iii
parts.scheme: M1: Uses integrating factor e^(-t) for dx/dt-x=-Ae^t. A1: Forms d(xe^(-t))/dt=-A. A1: Obtains xe^(-t)=-At+D. A1: Obtains x=(-At+D)e^t.

parts.label: b.i
parts.scheme: A1: Differentiates to d^2y/dt^2=-dx/dt+dy/dt. M1: Substitutes the a=-1 system equations. A1: Obtains d^2y/dt^2=2dy/dt.

parts.label: b.ii
parts.scheme: A1: Sets dY/dt=2Y. M1: Separates variables and integrates. A1: Obtains Y=Be^(2t).

parts.label: b.iii
parts.scheme: M1: Uses dy/dt=Be^(2t) and integrates. A1: Obtains y=(B/2)e^(2t)+C.

parts.label: b.iv
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes dy/dt and y into dy/dt=-x+y. A1: Rearranges to x=-(B/2)e^(2t)+C. A1: States the required x expression with a constant C.

parts.label: c.i
parts.scheme: M1: Differentiates dy/dt=-4x+y. M1: Eliminates x using the system equations. A1: Obtains d^2y/dt^2-2dy/dt-3y=0.

parts.label: c.ii
parts.scheme: A1: Differentiates y=Fe^(lambda t) to obtain the required first and second derivatives. M1: Substitutes into the differential equation and forms lambda^2-2lambda-3=0. A1: Solves the characteristic equation. A1: Obtains lambda values 3 and -1.

parts.label: c.iii
parts.scheme: A1: Differentiates y=Fe^(3t)+Ge^(-t) correctly once. A1: Differentiates it correctly twice. M1: Substitutes y, y' and y'' into d^2y/dt^2-2dy/dt-3y. A1: Simplifies to 0, verifying the solution.

parts.text: Prove general polygonal-number formula by induction.
parts.scheme: R1: Verifies both forms at n=1. M1: Assumes the formula true for n=k. M1: Writes Pr(k+1)=Pr(k)+1+k(r-2). A1: Substitutes the induction hypothesis into Pr(k+1). M1: Rearranges the numerator toward a k+1 expression. A1: Obtains [(r-2)(k+1)^2-(r-4)(k+1)]/2. A1: Establishes the induction step from k to k+1. R1: Concludes the formula holds for all positive integers n.

text: Continuous investigation of curved surface areas of cones, spheres and ellipsoids, using differentiation, transformations and definite integrals.

parts.label: a
parts.scheme: A1: Substitutes m=2 and h=3 into the cone surface-area integral. A1: Evaluates the integral to 18sqrt(5)pi.

parts.label: b.i
parts.scheme: A1: Deduces r=mh.

parts.label: b.ii
parts.scheme: M1: Uses Pythagoras for the cone slant height. A1: Obtains l=h sqrt(1+m^2).

parts.label: b.iii
parts.scheme: A1: Substitutes y=mx into the stated surface-area integral. M1: Integrates the resulting expression over 0 to h. A1: Rewrites the result as pi r l.

parts.label: c
parts.scheme: M1: Applies the chain rule or implicit differentiation. A1: Obtains dy/dx=-x/sqrt(r^2-x^2).

parts.label: d
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes the semicircle and derivative into the surface-area formula. A1: Forms the correct definite integral. M1: Simplifies the integrand to a constant r. A1: Evaluates the surface area as 4pi r^2.

parts.label: e.i
parts.scheme: A1: Identifies a horizontal stretch by factor 1/k. A1: States the invariant y-axis or equivalent complete transformation description.

parts.label: e.ii
parts.scheme: A1: States both intercepts x=plus or minus r/k.

parts.label: e.iii
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the chain rule or implicit differentiation for y=f(kx). A1: Obtains dy/dx=-k^2x/sqrt(r^2-k^2x^2).

parts.label: e.iv
parts.scheme: A1: Substitutes the semi-ellipse and derivative into the surface-area formula. M1: Simplifies the radical expression to form p(x). A1: Uses limits -r/k and r/k. A1: Obtains p(x)=r^2+(k^4-k^2)x^2.

parts.label: e.v
parts.scheme: A1: Chooses r=6378 km. A1: Chooses k=6378/6357. M1: Forms the definite integral for the Earth ellipsoid. A1: Obtains 5.101 times 10^8 km^2 to four significant figures.

parts.text: Sketch f1 and state its local maximum.

text: Continuous investigation of linear and quadratic functions whose coefficients and roots form arithmetic sequences.

parts.label: a
parts.scheme: A1: Finds r=1/2 for L(x)=2x-1. A1: Verifies 2,1/2,-1 form an arithmetic sequence.

parts.label: b.i
parts.scheme: A1: Derives r=-c/m.

parts.label: b.ii
parts.scheme: M1: Uses the arithmetic-sequence relation among m,r,c. A1: Substitutes r=-c/m correctly. M1: Eliminates the denominator to form the coefficient relation. A1: Obtains c=-m^2/(m+2).

parts.label: b.iii
parts.scheme: A1: States m is not -2 (and m is nonzero).

parts.label: c
parts.scheme: M1: Searches valid integer m systematically. A1: Obtains m=-4 or m=-3 with respective triples. A1: States L(x)=-4x+8 and L(x)=-3x+9.

parts.label: d.i
parts.scheme: A1: States r1+r2=-b/a.

parts.label: d.ii
parts.scheme: A1: States r1r2=c/a.

parts.label: e.i
parts.scheme: A1: States r2-r1=b-a.

parts.label: e.ii
parts.scheme: M1: Eliminates r2 using root sum and difference. A1: Obtains r1=(a^2-ab-b)/(2a).

parts.label: e.iii
parts.scheme: M1: Equates arithmetic-sequence forms for r1. M1: Simplifies to 2ab+b=0. A1: Concludes b=0 or a=-1/2.

parts.label: f
parts.scheme: A2: Expresses roots and c in terms of a when b=0. M1: Solves the resulting equation for a. A2: Obtains Q(x)=2x^2-2 and Q(x)=-2x^2+2.

parts.label: g.i
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes a=-1/2 into a valid root expression. A1: Obtains r1=(2b-1)/4.

parts.label: g.ii
parts.scheme: M1: Substitutes the root expression into Q(r1)=0 or an equivalent root relation. A1: Forms c=(4b+1)/2 and the quadratic 4b^2+20b+5=0. M1: Solves the quadratic in b. A1: Obtains b=(-5 plus or minus 2sqrt(5))/2. A1: Obtains c=(-9 plus or minus 4sqrt(5))/2.

solution.outline: AS-linear functions with integer coefficients are 2x-1, -4x+8 and -3x+9. AS-quadratic functions with b=0 are 2x^2-2 and -2x^2+2. For a=-1/2, b=(-5 plus or minus 2sqrt(5))/2 and c=(-9 plus or minus 4sqrt(5))/2.
